text:
United Health Services marks 45 years of growth and community healthcare service
Y. P. Sweet
United Health Services commemorated its 45th anniversary on Aug. 5, reflecting on decades of expansion, innovation, and community partnership since its formation in 1981.
The organization began with the merger of two local hospitals, aiming to provide quality healthcare close to home. Over the years, UHS has developed into a leading integrated healthcare system in the Southern Tier region. The system now includes four hospitals as well as physician practices, home care services, senior living facilities, outpatient and specialty services, graduate medical education programs, and numerous community partnerships.
UHS highlights that its progress is marked by milestones such as opening new facilities and introducing advanced technology to transform patient care. However, it emphasizes that its story is defined by the people who have contributed—physicians, nurses, therapists, technicians and other professionals—alongside administrative staff and volunteers who support daily operations. "Together, they built a culture of compassion, innovation and service that has touched generations across our region," the organization said.
The roots of UHS trace back before its official founding; Binghamton City Hospital opened in 1888 while another institution began in Lestershire (now Johnson City) in 1904 through a donation from George F. Johnson. These institutions not only provided medical care but also trained caregivers through nursing education programs starting in 1894.
A pivotal moment occurred on August 1, 1981, when Ideal/Wilson Medical Center joined with Binghamton General Hospital to form United Health Services. Since then, UHS has expanded services further by welcoming new hospitals into the system; developing senior living and home care programs; investing in outpatient care; modernizing technology such as Epic and MyChart; opening major facilities like UHS Wilson Main Tower; and establishing nationally recognized programs including trauma centers and specialized surgical certifications.
UHS underscores its ongoing commitment to meeting evolving community needs through educational partnerships with Binghamton University and SUNY campuses as well as public health initiatives during crises like COVID-19. It also supports food security efforts through collaborations with organizations such as CHOW and VINES.
Looking ahead, UHS plans continued investment in hospital-based neighborhoods for Chenango and Delaware counties along with modernization projects at existing facilities while prioritizing patient privacy initiatives.
